opus-5.5.text:
I think about it in two layers, and they're actually pretty connected.

The first layer is reliability. If you train a general-purpose robot policy purely from demonstrations, imitation learning gets you surprisingly far. You can get a model that does a lot of tasks at, say, sixty, seventy, eighty percent success. But for deployment, the gap between eighty and ninety-nine percent is everything. Nobody wants a robot that drops every fifth item or gets stuck in a corner it's never seen before. Imitation alone struggles there, because the demonstrations mostly show what success looks like. They don't really show the policy how to recover from its own mistakes, and they don't give it a signal for which of its behaviors actually lead to completing the task. Reinforcement learning gives you exactly that. You let the robot practice, you measure whether it succeeded, and you push the policy toward the things that work. That's how you grind out the long tail of failure modes. It's very similar to what we've seen with language models. Pretraining gives you broad competence, and RL on top gives you the precision and robustness you need to actually trust the system.

The second layer is new capabilities, which is the more exciting part scientifically. With demonstrations, you're fundamentally bounded by what a human teleoperator can show you. There are a lot of tasks where that's a real ceiling: really dynamic motions, things that need fast reactive control, tasks where the human operator is just clumsy through the teleop interface. RL lets the robot discover strategies that nobody demonstrated. We've seen that for years in simulation and in more narrow settings, things like in-hand manipulation or locomotion, where RL finds solutions that are frankly better than what you'd hand-design or teleoperate.

What's changed now is that we have these large pretrained foundation models as a starting point. Ten years ago, doing RL on a real robot from scratch was painfully sample inefficient. You'd spend weeks of robot time to learn one skill. Now you start from a policy that already roughly knows what it's doing, so exploration is much more focused, and you can fine-tune with comparatively little real-world experience. And as these models get better at judging their own progress, using vision-language models as reward models or success detectors, the bottleneck of hand-specifying rewards starts to shrink too.

So the picture I have in my head is a loop: broad pretraining on lots of data, deploy, let the robots collect experience, use RL to improve both reliability on the tasks you care about and to stretch into things you couldn't demonstrate, and then feed that back into the next generation of the model. I don't think we're fully there yet, there are hard open problems around safe exploration in the real world, reward specification, and doing this at scale across many robots. But I'm pretty convinced that's the direction that gets us to robots that are genuinely useful and not just impressive in a demo.

r001.rationale: The response says human demonstrations limit what a robot can learn to do, but it does not argue that scaling human-collected data alone cannot indefinitely improve robots’ initial policies.

r002.rationale: It says robot-collected experience can improve a policy and feed into the next generation, but does not identify deployment data as a valuable source of pre-training data.

r003.rationale: The response describes robots collecting experience, but does not predict increasing reliance on autonomous data collection to build training datasets.

r004.rationale: It identifies scaling across many robots as an open problem and says the field is not fully there yet, but does not clearly state that learning from robots’ own experience has not been demonstrated at a scale that convincingly supports deployment.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of RL as playing two quite different roles, and it's worth separating them.

The first is reliability. Most of what we deploy today starts from imitation learning — you collect demonstrations, you train a policy, and you get something that works maybe 70 or 80 percent of the time on the distribution it was trained on. The problem is that last stretch. The failures aren't random; they cluster in states the demonstrator never visited, because a human teleoperator doesn't make the mistakes the policy makes, so there's no data for recovering from them. RL is the natural tool for closing that gap. You let the policy act, you reward success and penalize failure, and it learns to recover from its own errors rather than someone else's. In practice that's often a fairly conservative loop: a small amount of on-robot interaction on top of a strong pretrained prior, with the goal of pushing a task from "mostly works" to "works reliably enough that you'd leave the room." That's not glamorous, but it's where most of the deployment value sits right now.

The second role is capability, and that's where I think people sometimes underestimate RL. Imitation can only ever get you to roughly human-demonstrator level, and for a lot of manipulation — fast, contact-rich, dynamic things — humans teleoperating through a controller are actually quite bad. RL can find strategies the demonstrator never showed, because the robot's body and sensors are different from ours. You see this in locomotion already, where learned controllers are far more robust than anything hand-designed. I expect the same in manipulation once we have reward signals that are cheap to obtain at scale — learned success detectors, vision-language models judging outcomes, and so on.

The key to making both of these work in a general-purpose setting is not throwing away what you have. You start from a broad, pretrained foundation model that gives you language grounding and a reasonable prior over actions, and you use RL to fine-tune it on the robot without collapsing that generality. Getting that balance right — improving on specific tasks while retaining breadth — is honestly the central technical problem, and I think it's where a lot of the interesting work in the next couple of years will be.

r001.rationale: The response says imitation can only reach roughly the human demonstrator’s level and that demonstrators miss the policy’s failure states, communicating a limit to improvement from human demonstrations alone.

r002.rationale: It discusses on-robot interaction for fine-tuning, but does not predict that data gathered during deployments will become valuable pre-training data.

r003.rationale: The response describes a small amount of on-robot RL interaction, but does not predict increasing reliance on autonomous data collection to build training datasets.

r004.rationale: It does not state that learning from robots’ own experience remains unproven at a scale that convincingly supports deployment.

astra-6.text:
I think reinforcement learning can contribute in two fairly different ways. One is to make a capability you already have much more reliable. Getting a robot to do something once is very different from getting it to do it consistently when the object moves, the lighting changes, or a grasp doesn’t quite work. Reinforcement learning gives you a way to optimize for actually completing the task, including recovering from mistakes, rather than just reproducing the actions in a demonstration.

The other is to discover behavior that’s difficult to demonstrate or specify directly. You might be able to describe what success looks like without knowing the sequence of movements that gets you there. Through interaction, a robot can potentially learn strategies that weren’t present in its training demonstrations.

But the difficult part is making that interaction practical. On a real robot, exploration takes time, hardware wears out, and some mistakes are unacceptable. So I’d expect a combination of learning from existing data, practicing in simulation, and carefully constrained learning on hardware. And we should distinguish improving average performance from establishing deployment reliability. Reinforcement learning can help with both, but a higher reward alone doesn’t establish that a robot is ready to operate safely in somebody’s home.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts task completion with reproducing demonstrations, but does not argue that scaling human-collected data alone cannot indefinitely improve initial policies.

r002.rationale: It does not predict that deployment-collected data will become valuable pre-training data.

r003.rationale: It discusses learning through interaction but does not predict growing reliance on autonomous data collection for training datasets.

r004.rationale: It notes practical limits of real-robot exploration, but does not state that robot-experience learning lacks a convincing demonstration at deployment-supporting scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reinforcement learning has a role in both, and they’re closely connected. A robot can demonstrate a skill once and still be very far from something you would want to deploy. It needs to work across different objects, different environments, and situations where something goes wrong. Reinforcement learning gives us a way to optimize for actually completing the task, including learning how to recover when the first attempt fails.

For new capabilities, the exciting part is that the robot can improve through interaction. Demonstrations give it a starting point, but they don’t necessarily define the limit of what it can learn. Through trial and error, it can discover strategies that weren’t explicitly demonstrated.

The challenge is making that process practical. Real-world experience is expensive, and exploration has to be safe. So I see reinforcement learning working alongside demonstrations, simulation, and pretrained models. Those provide a strong foundation; reinforcement learning can then help turn that foundation into behavior that is more capable and more dependable.
